title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 45–46
description: Curated upper-intermediate speaking verbs, reporting patterns, tone adverbs, sensory vocabulary, touch, smell, taste and sight distinctions.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching pages for Units 45–46, labelled reporting verb and loudness tables, language help, exercises 45.1–45.5 and 46.1–46.7, and corresponding answer-key entries reviewed for vocabulary and grammar.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA included for straightforward lexical items. Multi-word expressions sometimes omit IPA rather than presenting an uncertain connected-speech transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Source and answer-key review, original example drafting, meaning and collocation checks, static reference-schema matching, provenance and word-versus-sentence audio text checks. No live UI import or browser audio test.
audit.limitations: An empty audio field means no bundled recording. Browser TTS, microphone recognition and live VocabLab import have not been tested.

units.title: Unit 45 — Speaking
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 96–97 (PDF pages 97–98).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish quiet, loud, unclear and high-pitched manners of speaking and the attitudes they may suggest.
Use accurate reporting-verb patterns with about, on, to, with, that-clauses and infinitives.
Choose speech adverbs that express anger, sadness, happiness, concern and reluctance.
Recognise when speech verbs describe a momentary situation versus a speech difficulty.

items.example: She whispered the answer so that nobody else could hear.
items.note: Very quiet speech, often for secrecy or to avoid disturbing others.

items.example: My friend whispered in my ear during the performance.
items.note: The preposition in is usual when someone whispers into another person's ear.

items.example: He murmured a gentle reply without looking up.
items.note: Soft, often quiet or affectionate speech; unlike mumble, it need not be unclear.

items.example: She mumbled her name and the receptionist asked her to repeat it.
items.note: Quiet and difficult-to-understand speech, sometimes caused by nervousness.

items.example: He muttered a complaint as he left the room.
items.note: Usually quiet speech, often signalling irritation or resentment.

items.example: He muttered under his breath when the meeting was extended.
items.note: A useful expression for speaking quietly enough that others may not hear.

items.example: The instructor shouted instructions over the engine noise.
items.note: Loud speech, commonly used for anger, excitement or distance.

items.example: A passer-by shouted for help when she saw the accident.
items.note: A natural collocation for calling loudly for assistance.

items.example: The child screamed when the lights suddenly went out.
items.note: Very loud cry, often expressing fear or excitement; words are not always present.

items.example: She shrieked with laughter at the unexpected joke.
items.note: A particularly high-pitched, piercing cry, often from fright or amusement.

items.example: He stuttered briefly while introducing himself.
items.note: Speech with repeated or interrupted sounds; it can also be a persistent speech difference.

items.example: She stammered an apology after forgetting the visitor's name.
items.note: Often interchangeable with stutter; neither automatically means the speaker is nervous.

items.example: He boasted to his colleagues about his promotion.
items.note: Common pattern: boast to someone about something; can also introduce a that-clause.

items.example: She kept boasting about the number of awards she had won.
items.note: Boasting implies excessive pride in an achievement or possession.

items.example: Several passengers complained to the manager about the delay.
items.note: Complain to a person about an issue; do not use complain of someone in this pattern.

items.example: People complained about the lack of clear information.
items.note: About identifies what causes dissatisfaction.

items.example: The researcher insisted that the results were accurate.
items.note: Insist that + clause conveys a firm claim; insist on + noun or -ing demands an action.

items.example: They insist on using reusable containers at every event.
items.note: After insist on, use a noun or an -ing form, not a bare infinitive.

items.example: She maintained that the original estimate was correct.
items.note: Formal reporting verb: maintain that + clause means assert confidently, not physically maintain equipment.

items.example: Several residents objected to the proposed building.
items.note: Object to + noun or -ing expresses opposition; distinct from the noun object.

items.example: I object to paying extra for a service I never requested.
items.note: The to here is a preposition and must be followed by -ing, not an infinitive.

items.example: He confessed that he had changed the figures.
items.note: Confess that + clause reports an admission, often about wrongdoing.

items.example: She confessed to breaking the laboratory window.
items.note: Alternative pattern: confess to + -ing; do not say confess to break.

items.example: The customer threatened to report the company.
items.note: Threaten to + infinitive reports a stated intention to take unwelcome action.

items.example: The doctor urged her to get more rest.
items.note: Urge someone to do something is strong encouragement or advice.

items.example: The neighbours argued with each other about the noise.
items.note: Argue with someone about something: the people and issue take different prepositions.

items.example: I do not want to argue with you about this decision.
items.note: With introduces the other participant in a disagreement.

items.example: He begged the organisers to let him enter the competition.
items.note: Beg someone to do something is stronger and more desperate than ask.

items.example: The injured runner groaned that his ankle hurt.
items.note: Groan can report spoken words expressing pain, despair or frustration.

items.example: The staff grumbled about the new working hours.
items.note: Grumble about something means complain in a dissatisfied, often low-key way.

items.example: She spoke angrily after hearing the accusation.
items.note: A speech adverb describing a strong feeling of anger.

items.example: He replied furiously when he discovered the mistake.
items.note: Expresses greater intensity than angrily in this context.

items.example: He spoke bitterly about how his former employer treated him.
items.note: Conveys lasting resentment or hurt, not necessarily a raised voice.

items.example: She remarked gloomily that the forecast looked terrible.
items.note: A pessimistic, low-spirited manner of speaking.

items.example: He answered miserably after failing the driving test.
items.note: Conveys unhappiness or distress in the speaker's tone.

items.example: They said sadly that the shop was closing.
items.note: An ordinary adverb for an unhappy tone.

items.example: She announced happily that she had passed the exam.
items.note: Signals obvious happiness in the way someone speaks.

items.example: The guide cheerfully welcomed everyone on board.
items.note: Suggests lively, positive friendliness rather than simply contentment.

items.example: I would gladly explain the procedure again.
items.note: Often describes willingness as well as happy agreement.

items.example: She said hopefully that the weather might improve.
items.note: In this use, the speaker's tone expresses hope for a good outcome.

items.example: He asked anxiously whether the patient was safe.
items.note: Expresses worry and uncertainty in the speaker's voice.

items.example: The applicant answered nervously at first.
items.note: Often describes unease in a stressful or unfamiliar situation.

items.example: She cried desperately for somebody to call an ambulance.
items.note: An urgent or intensely worried manner, much stronger than merely nervous.

items.example: They talked excitedly about the upcoming trip.
items.note: Typically a high-energy voice when something exciting is happening.

items.example: The customer asked impatiently when the order would arrive.
items.note: Signals annoyance at having to wait or tolerate a delay.

items.example: He reluctantly agreed to take the later train.
items.note: Means with little willingness, not with excitement.

items.example: She smiled shyly before giving her presentation.
items.note: Indicates reserve or lack of confidence in an interaction.

B: Describing feelings and reporting verb patterns

units.title: Unit 46 — The six senses
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 98–99 (PDF pages 99–100).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Use look, sound, taste, feel and smell with adjectives to report sensory impressions.
Distinguish glance, observe, glimpse, peer, gaze, stare and witness according to duration, purpose and context.
Describe loudness, taste, touch and smell with precise gradations and collocations.
Understand taste-related adjective contrasts and discuss claimed sixth-sense phenomena accurately.

items.example: Her sight improved after she got new glasses.
items.note: The ability to see; one of the five physical senses.

items.example: His hearing was affected by years of loud music.
items.note: The sense that allows us to detect sounds.

items.example: A blocked nose can affect your sense of taste.
items.note: The sense used to recognise flavours; also a verb meaning have a flavour.

items.example: The material felt soft to the touch.
items.note: The physical sense that detects pressure and texture.

items.example: Dogs have a very sensitive sense of smell.
items.note: The ability to detect odours; smell is also a verb and a noun for an odour.

items.pt: parecer horrível; estar com aparência péssima
items.example: The old building looks dreadful after the storm.
items.note: After linking verbs such as look, use an adjective, not an adverb, to describe an appearance.

items.example: Your holiday plans sound marvellous.
items.note: Sound + adjective describes an impression from hearing information.

items.example: The sauce tastes good with fresh herbs.
items.note: Taste takes an adjective as a linking verb: tastes good, not tastes well in this sense.

items.pt: parecer estranho ao tato; causar sensação estranha
items.example: The fabric feels strange against my skin.
items.note: Feel + adjective describes a physical impression or condition.

items.example: The bread smells delicious straight from the oven.
items.note: Smell + adjective describes a perceived odour.

items.example: She claims to have a sixth sense about approaching danger.
items.note: A supposed awareness outside the five physical senses.

items.example: The documentary explored claims of extrasensory perception.
items.note: A formal term for supposed perception beyond the five senses; not an established physical sense.

items.example: I could see the lighthouse from the ferry.
items.note: The broad, unmarked verb for visual perception, unlike peer or glimpse.

items.example: She glanced at the clock during the presentation.
items.note: A quick look, often followed by at or through.

items.example: I noticed a loose screw near the panel.
items.note: To become aware of something, not necessarily after looking deliberately.

items.example: The students observed the birds through binoculars.
items.note: Watching carefully or systematically, as in scientific observation.

items.example: I glimpsed a deer before it disappeared into the trees.
items.note: A brief or incomplete sighting, often by chance.

items.example: He peered through the fog to read the street sign.
items.note: Looking closely because something is difficult to see.

items.example: They gazed at the stars for several minutes.
items.note: A long, steady look, often expressing interest or admiration.

items.example: Please stop staring at the stranger across the table.
items.note: A fixed, prolonged look that can seem rude, intense or surprised.

items.example: Two passengers witnessed the collision.
items.note: To see an event as it happens, especially an accident or crime.

items.pt: espiar através de; olhar atentamente por
items.example: She peered through the narrow gap in the curtain.
items.note: Through introduces a small opening or an obscuring surface.

items.example: We gazed at the waterfall in silence.
items.note: Gaze at something is a natural prepositional pattern.

items.example: The child stared at the unusual machine.
items.note: At introduces the focus of a fixed look.

items.example: The electric motor was almost noiseless at low speed.
items.note: At the very quiet end of the loudness scale; practically no sound.

items.example: The audience remained silent before the performance.
items.note: Not making or speaking any sound in the context.

items.example: We moved to a quieter room to study.
items.note: Relatively little noise, but not necessarily complete silence.

items.example: The old fan became noisy after a few months.
items.note: Producing a lot of sound, often unwanted.

items.example: The music was so loud that we could not talk.
items.note: High sound volume; not necessarily unpleasant by definition.

items.example: There was a deafening roar when the engines started.
items.note: Extremely loud; stronger than noisy or loud.

items.example: The ripe mango tasted sweet without any added sugar.
items.note: Basic taste commonly associated with sugar and honey.

items.example: The soup is too salty for my liking.
items.note: Tasting of salt; a common description of seawater or crisps.

items.example: Unsweetened coffee can taste quite bitter.
items.note: The flavour associated with some coffee or dark vegetables.

items.example: The lemonade was too sour until she added sugar.
items.note: Acidic taste, common in limes and vinegar.

items.example: The noodles were spicy but full of flavour.
items.note: Flavoured with strong spices; does not always imply high temperature.

items.example: He ordered a hot curry with plenty of chilli.
items.note: Hot can refer to strong chilli heat, not just food temperature.

items.example: I prefer a mild curry that does not burn my mouth.
items.note: Opposite of hot when describing the strength of a curry.

items.example: The vegetable stew was simple but tasty.
items.note: Positive judgement of food flavour; unlike tasteful, it does not describe elegant design.

items.example: The apartment has tasteful furniture and subtle colours.
items.note: Appropriate for decor, architecture or style, not a synonym of delicious food.

items.example: The rice was badly cooked and the vegetables were tasteless.
items.note: In food, tasteless means lacking flavour; not necessarily offensive.

items.example: The hotel lobby had expensive but tasteless decor.
items.note: In design or behaviour, tasteless means lacking good aesthetic or social judgement.

items.example: He poked me gently in the shoulder to get my attention.
items.note: A short push with a finger or pointed object, often to attract attention.

items.example: She stroked the kitten's fur until it fell asleep.
items.note: To move your hand gently across a surface, usually affectionately.

items.example: The trainer patted the dog on its head.
items.note: Repeated gentle touches with the palm, unlike a long stroke.

items.pt: dar uma batidinha; tocar de leve
items.example: A colleague tapped me on the shoulder to interrupt.
items.note: A quick, light touch or knock, usually brief.

items.example: He grasped the railing as he climbed the stairs.
items.note: To take or hold something tightly and firmly.

items.example: She grabbed her coat and hurried outside.
items.note: To take something suddenly or quickly, often in a hurry.

items.example: Someone snatched his bag while he was waiting for the bus.
items.note: To seize something suddenly, often from another person's possession.

items.example: Press the green button to begin the test.
items.note: Apply pressure to a surface or control, rather than simply touch it.

items.example: Please handle the glass equipment carefully.
items.note: To hold, move or work with something physically.

items.example: All delicate instruments must be handled with care.
items.note: Common instruction for fragile objects; handle is a verb.

items.example: The rubbish bin was stinking after several hot days.
items.note: Very strong unpleasant smell; informal and vivid.

items.example: The drain gave off a foul-smelling gas.
items.note: Describes something that emits an extremely unpleasant odour.

items.example: The rotten fruit gave off a putrid smell.
items.note: Strongly suggests decay and rotting material.

items.example: The books smelled musty after years in a damp attic.
items.note: Unpleasant stale smell from old or slightly damp places.

items.example: A pungent smell of garlic filled the kitchen.
items.note: Very strong and sharp odour; can be unpleasant but not necessarily.

items.example: The fragrant flowers scented the garden at night.
items.note: Describes a pleasant, often delicate scent.

items.example: Freshly chopped herbs are especially aromatic.
items.note: Pleasant and noticeable smell, often associated with herbs and cooking.

items.example: The sweet-smelling soap was made with lavender.
items.note: A pleasant smell, often like flowers or perfume.

items.example: She used perfumed lotion after showering.
items.note: Often means that fragrance has been added to a product.

items.example: The hotel placed scented candles in the entrance hall.
items.note: Describes products or objects with an added pleasant fragrance.

items.example: The film features characters who claim to communicate through telepathy.
items.note: Claimed awareness of another person's thoughts or feelings without ordinary senses; not scientifically established as a reliable ability.

items.example: She had a premonition that something unexpected was about to happen.
items.note: A feeling or supposed advance knowledge of an event before it happens.

items.example: Her intuition told her to question the unusually low price.
items.note: Understanding or judgement that seems immediate rather than consciously reasoned.

items.pt: déjà-vu; sensação de já ter vivido algo
items.example: Walking down the unfamiliar street gave me a strong sense of déjà vu.
items.note: A sensation that a present experience has happened before, although you cannot explain why.
